description: Educational wiki structure. status: complete = full textbook text with references; outline = learning objectives, section outline, key terms, a short introduction and verified references, full text scheduled for Phase 2; planned = topic reserved.

units.title: Cyanobacteria: Biology, Ecology, and Harmful Freshwater Blooms
units.summary: A ten-chapter undergraduate text on the photosynthetic bacteria that shaped Earth's atmosphere, dominate many nutrient-rich waters today, and can produce toxins that matter for people, pets and livestock in Kentucky.

units.title: Nitrogen and Phosphorus in Freshwater
units.summary: Forms, sources and transformations of N and P from field to stream. Begins in Chapter 4 of the cyanobacteria unit.

units.title: Freshwater Food Webs
units.summary: Producers, grazers, predators and decomposers in streams and ponds. Begins in Chapter 6 of the cyanobacteria unit.

units.title: Aquatic Microbiology
units.summary: Biofilms, plankton and microbial interactions. Begins in Chapter 3 of the cyanobacteria unit.

units.title: Watersheds and Karst
units.summary: How water moves across and beneath the south-central Kentucky landscape. Begins on the Watersheds & Maps page.

records.title: What Are Cyanobacteria?
records.summary: Photosynthetic bacteria, not algae: cell structure, oxygenic photosynthesis, pigments, and their role in Earth's oxygenation and the origin of chloroplasts.
learning_objectives: Explain why cyanobacteria are classified as bacteria even though they are often called blue-green algae.
Compare the cellular organization of a cyanobacterium with that of a eukaryotic green alga.
Describe oxygenic photosynthesis and the roles of chlorophyll a, phycobiliproteins and thylakoid membranes.
Summarize the evidence linking cyanobacteria to the rise of atmospheric oxygen and to the origin of chloroplasts.
Describe the ecological roles of cyanobacteria as primary producers and nitrogen fixers.

records.title: Cyanobacterial Diversity and Identification
records.summary: Unicellular, colonial and filamentous forms; heterocytes, akinetes and gas vesicles; eight freshwater genera; why names change; and the limits of identification by microscope.
learning_objectives: Distinguish unicellular, colonial and filamentous growth forms.
Identify heterocytes, akinetes, gas vesicles and mucilage and explain the function of each.
Recognize diagnostic features of eight common freshwater genera.
Explain why genus names such as Anabaena and Cylindrospermopsis have changed.
Explain why microscopic identification cannot determine species with certainty or show whether a population produces toxins.

records.title: Freshwater Ecology of Cyanobacteria
records.summary: Planktonic versus benthic life; light, temperature, mixing and residence time; succession, competition, grazing and microbial partners — from shaded streams to sunlit ponds.
learning_objectives: Contrast planktonic and benthic cyanobacteria and the habitats each occupies.
Explain how light, temperature, stratification and water residence time favor or limit cyanobacteria.
Predict how a shaded, flowing stream and an open, still pond differ in their likely cyanobacterial communities.
Describe seasonal succession and the roles of competition, grazing and microbial interactions.

records.title: Nutrient Cycling and Agricultural Watersheds
records.summary: Nitrogen and phosphorus forms, limitation and co-limitation, eutrophication, and how fertilizer, manure, soil, wastewater and stormwater reach water — and when they don't.
learning_objectives: Describe the major forms of nitrogen and phosphorus in fresh water and how they transform.
Explain nutrient limitation and co-limitation and why single-nutrient explanations of blooms are often wrong.
Identify external and internal nutrient sources in a watershed.
Distinguish proximity to farmland from hydrologic connectivity, including in karst.

records.title: Harmful Algal Blooms
records.summary: What a bloom is, why some are harmful, the four major cyanotoxin groups, oxygen depletion, health effects, U.S. guidance values and how Kentucky issues advisories.
learning_objectives: Define a bloom and explain why bloom, harmful bloom and toxic bloom are different claims.
Compare microcystins, anatoxins, cylindrospermopsins and saxitoxins by target and producer.
Distinguish intracellular from dissolved toxin and explain why it matters for sampling and treatment.
Explain why cell counts, color and toxin concentration are related but not interchangeable.
Find and interpret current Kentucky advisories and U.S. EPA guidance values.

records.title: Cyanobacteria and Aquatic Food Webs
records.summary: How green algae, diatoms, rotifers, copepods, Daphnia, snails, fish and decomposers interact with cyanobacteria — and why cyanobacteria are hard to eat.
learning_objectives: Place cyanobacteria in a freshwater food web alongside green algae and diatoms.
Explain why cyanobacteria are often poor food: nutrition, shape, toxins and digestive inhibitors.
Describe evidence for naturally tolerant Daphnia populations and the role of gut microbiota.

records.title: Bloom Prevention and Biological Control
records.summary: Nutrient management, restoration, buffers, mixing, algaecides, biomanipulation, grazer–cyanobacteria coevolution, microbiomes — and a careful look at engineered organisms.
learning_objectives: Explain why reducing nutrient inputs is the foundation of bloom prevention.
Evaluate in-lake measures (mixing, algaecides, hydrogen peroxide) and their limits.
Describe biomanipulation and the conditions under which it succeeds or fails.
Distinguish contained laboratory research with modified organisms from environmental release, and outline ecological risk assessment.

records.title: Studying Cyanobacteria in the Laboratory
records.summary: Wet mounts, brightfield microscopy, calibration and photomicrography, metadata, water chemistry, pigments, molecular concepts and toxin testing — with the limits and safety rules for each.
learning_objectives: Prepare and document a wet mount with calibrated measurements.
Record the environmental metadata that make an observation useful.
Explain what pigment, molecular and toxin methods can and cannot tell you.
Apply the safety rules for handling potentially toxic environmental samples.

records.title: Cyanobacteria in Kentucky
records.summary: What is documented about blooms in Kentucky's reservoirs, rivers and ponds since 2013, the agricultural and karst setting, and how much remains unknown near Somerset.
learning_objectives: Summarize documented Kentucky HAB events and how advisories are issued.
Describe Kentucky's freshwater settings: large reservoirs, the Ohio River, small lakes and farm ponds, karst streams.
Distinguish documented Kentucky findings from hypotheses about Allen Branch or Lake Cumberland.

records.title: Open Research Questions
records.summary: Undergraduate-scale research directions for Allen Branch and other south-central Kentucky waters, each linked to background, methods and references.
learning_objectives: Turn a topic into a testable research question and hypothesis.
Match a question to feasible methods and an appropriate site.
Recognize what a first-year dataset can and cannot show.
